096.subtitle: A face assembled name by name, and then declared too fine to see

commentary.meaning: Nine names, and the verse is built as an ascent that turns into a disappearance. The first line is almost entirely a face: a lovely face, a lotus, beautiful brows, splendour — four names of visible beauty, with only the fifth stepping back to say that the gods follow where she leads. The second line begins in the same visual register and then leaves it. Her throat is dark, which is not a beauty mark but a mark of what Śiva swallowed for the world's sake; she possesses radiance, which the hymn has already given her sixteen names earlier as a bare noun and now gives again with a different grammar; she is the agitator, the one who shakes what has settled; and the last name says that her form is subtle, too fine for any sense to lay hold of. That ending is the argument of the verse. It has spent eight names building something the eye could hold — brows, cheek, throat, radiance — and then, in the ninth, it withdraws the whole construction, which is exactly what a meditation on a deity's form is trained to do.
commentary.history:
The first line's names are the common currency of Sanskrit description, and they gain their force from placement rather than novelty. Sumukhī, lovely-faced, is a plain possessive compound; so is subhrūḥ, which uses bhrū, the eyebrow, one of the small class of nouns that resist a separate feminine and simply stay as they are. The eyebrow is a technical piece of Sanskrit poetic equipment: it is the arc against which the bow of Kāma is measured, and the space between the brows is where meditation is directed and where this hymn locates one of the centres of the body. Nalinī, lotus, comes from nalina, and behind that lies nala, a hollow reed or stalk — the plant is named for the tube that carries it to the surface. The word means the plant, the flower, and by extension the whole pond crowded with them, so the name is at once a comparison for her face and a picture of the water she rises out of.

Suranāyikā is the one name in the first line that is about rank rather than appearance, and both its halves have histories. Sura, a god, is almost certainly a back-formation: the old Vedic word asura, meaning lord and used of the highest gods, came to be heard as a-sura, "non-god", and a positive sura was then invented to fill the gap the false negative had opened. Nāyikā is the feminine of nāyaka, leader, and in the technical language of Sanskrit drama and poetics the nāyikā is the heroine, the woman around whom the emotional action turns. Both senses are live. She leads the gods, and she is the heroine of the story the gods are in.

Kālakaṇṭhī is the verse's one mythological name and its darkest. When the gods and the demons churned the ocean for the nectar of immortality, what came up before the nectar was a poison so virulent that it threatened to destroy the three worlds. Śiva drank it. In the most widely repeated version his wife caught his throat with her hand to keep it from going further down, so that it stayed lodged there and stained it, and he has been Nīlakaṇṭha, the blue-throated, ever since. To apply the feminine form of that epithet to her is to make one of two claims, and the commentators use both. Either she is not different from him, so that his marks are hers; or she was the reason the poison stopped where it did, and the dark throat is as much a record of her act as of his. Kāla means black and also means Time, and the hymn is entirely capable of intending a name to be heard twice.

Kṣobhiṇī comes from a root meaning to shake, to agitate, to throw into commotion — the word is used of a churned ocean, the same field of imagery as the name before it. In this school it is also a term of art. Kṣobha is the disturbance of a perfect equilibrium without which nothing can be manifested at all: creation begins as an agitation, not as an act of will, and the tradition's ritual vocabulary accordingly gives the name Sarvasaṃkṣobhiṇī, the all-agitating, to one of the hand-signs used in worship and to figures in the enclosures of the Śrīcakra. The name is not saying that she causes trouble. It is saying that she is the reason anything moves at all, which includes whatever unsettles a settled practitioner.

Sūkṣma, the last word of the verse, is the standard technical opposite of sthūla, gross. Sanskrit philosophy uses the pair for the gross and subtle elements, for the gross and subtle bodies, and for the two levels at which anything can be said to exist. Śrīvidyā applies the distinction to the goddess herself: she is generally taught to have a gross form, which is the figure described in the meditation verse with her noose, goad, bow and arrows; a subtle form, which is the mantra; and a form beyond both. On that reading sūkṣmarūpiṇī is not a vague statement about her being hard to see. It is a specific claim that the sound the reciter is producing is a body of hers, no less than the face the first line of this verse has just finished describing.

One more thing about this verse is worth naming, because it becomes visible only when a reader is far enough into the hymn. Kāntiḥ was given as a name sixteen names ago, and kāntimatī is given here; śāntiḥ was given in the same recent group, and śāntimatī appears far earlier in the text. The hymn reaches a thousand partly by taking a word and turning it over — as a bare abstract noun, as a possessive, as a compound — and a reader who suspects padding should notice that the grammar changes the claim each time. To be radiance and to possess radiance are not the same statement.
commentary.practice:
The verse divides by sound as cleanly as any in the hymn. Four of the five names in the first line begin with the sibilant s or ś; three of the four in the second begin with k. Reciters who have just come through the six ku- names a few verses earlier will recognise the technique. Use it: if you lose your place here, you have lost it inside a block of s-names or of k-names, which narrows the search considerably.

Subhrūḥ is the hardest syllable in the verse and one of the hardest in the hymn. It is a single syllable: bh, an aspirated labial released as one sound, then r, then a long ū, then the light breath of the visarga. It is not bhu-rū, and there is no vowel between the bh and the r. Slow it down, hold the ū, and let the visarga be an exhalation, not a syllable. In archanā this name becomes subhruve — the ū-stem takes -ve — which is one of the handful of places in the thousand where the familiar -āyai does not appear.

The verse continues the lesson in retroflex assimilation that the preceding one set up. Nalinī and kāntimatī keep the dental n of the feminine suffix; kṣobhiṇī and sūkṣmarūpiṇī have the retroflex ṇ. The trigger in both is the retroflex sibilant ṣ inside the conjunct kṣ, exactly as an r triggers it elsewhere. Nothing is arbitrary, and the contrast is audible if the consonants are given their proper places.

Kālakaṇṭhī contains ṇṭh: a retroflex nasal followed by an aspirated retroflex stop, the tongue curled well back for both, with the breath released on the ṭh. Kṣobhiṇī and sūkṣmarūpiṇī each begin or turn on kṣ, and in sūkṣma the conjunct is followed immediately by m, giving a three-consonant sequence in the middle of the word: sūk-ṣma, with the long ū before it carrying the weight of the syllable. Śobhanā opens with the palatal ś, made further forward than the retroflex ṣ of kṣobhiṇī, and the two sibilants should not collapse into one another.

What the verse asks of the person chanting it is a small exercise in letting go, and the order of the names supplies it. Meditation on a deity in this tradition proceeds by construction: the practitioner assembles the figure detail by detail, face, brows, throat, ornaments, until it stands complete and stable, and only then dissolves it into the mantra or into a point of light. This verse performs that sequence in sixteen syllables per line. A reciter can follow it deliberately — hold the face through the first line, hold the dark throat and the radiance through most of the second, and then, at sūkṣmarūpiṇī, let the picture go and attend only to the sound.

The kṣobhiṇī immediately before it makes that easier rather than harder. Something has to unsettle the image before it can be released, and the hymn has named the unsettling as hers too. Practitioners who have found their concentration breaking up at exactly the point where it seemed most secure will recognise the sequence, and may find it useful that the text treats the disturbance not as a failure of attention but as the next name.

crossReferences.iast: sudhām apy āsvādya pratibhayajarāmṛtyuhariṇīṃ vipadyante viśve vidhiśatamakhādyā diviṣadaḥ | karālaṃ yat kṣvelaṃ kabalitavataḥ kālakalanā na śambhos tanmūlaṃ tava janani tāṭaṅkamahimā ||
crossReferences.translation: Though they have drunk the nectar that takes away the terror of old age and death, all the dwellers in heaven perish in the end — the Creator, the god of a hundred sacrifices, and the rest. But Śambhu, who swallowed the appalling poison, is not counted by Time; and the root of that, mother, is the power of your ear-ornaments.
crossReferences.relevance: The episode behind kālakaṇṭhī, told with the credit assigned where this hymn also tends to assign it. The poem takes the same two facts — he drank the poison, he is untouched by death — and traces them to her, specifically to the ornaments that mark her as a wife whose husband will not die. Note the pun the poem is working, kāla as both the poison's blackness and Time; our name carries it too.

crossReferences.deva: एष सर्वेषु भूतेषु गूढोऽऽत्मा न प्रकाशते । दृश्यते त्वग्र्यया बुद्ध्या सूक्ष्मया सूक्ष्मदर्शिभिः ॥
crossReferences.iast: eṣa sarveṣu bhūteṣu gūḍho 'tmā na prakāśate | dṛśyate tv agryayā buddhyā sūkṣmayā sūkṣmadarśibhiḥ ||
crossReferences.translation: Hidden in all beings, this self does not shine forth; but it is seen by those who see subtly, with a keen and subtle understanding.
crossReferences.relevance: The classical use of sūkṣma, and the reason the last name of our verse is not a way of saying that she is vague. The Upaniṣad's point is that subtlety is a property of the instrument as much as of the object: what is subtle is seen by a subtle faculty. Applied to sūkṣmarūpiṇī, it makes the closing name a demand on the reciter rather than a disclaimer about the goddess.

references.title: The Saundaryalaharī, or Flood of Beauty
references.author: ed. and tr. W. Norman Brown (Harvard Oriental Series 43, 1958)
references.note: Still the most careful English edition of the poem, with the Sanskrit, a literal translation and notes that record where the commentators disagree. Brown is also frank about the yantras and ritual uses attached to each verse, which most devotional editions either omit or present without comment.

references.title: The Secret of the Three Cities: An Introduction to Hindu Śākta Tantrism
references.author: Douglas Renfrew Brooks (University of Chicago Press, 1990)
references.note: The place to read about the gross, subtle and supreme forms of the goddess and why the tradition holds that the mantra is a body rather than a description of one. That teaching is what turns sūkṣmarūpiṇī from a poetic hedge into a technical statement.

references.title: The Principal Upaniṣads
references.author: ed. and tr. S. Radhakrishnan (George Allen & Unwin, 1953)
references.note: Convenient because it prints the Sanskrit, a transliteration and a translation together, which is what a reader wants when checking a single verse like the one on subtle seeing. Radhakrishnan's interpretive notes lean Vedāntic and should be read as one voice rather than as the text's own.

references.title: The Practical Sanskrit-English Dictionary
references.author: Vaman Shivram Apte (revised enlarged edition, Poona, 1957-59)
references.note: Better than Monier-Williams for the poetic vocabulary of this verse, because Apte quotes the classical poets. The entries for bhrū, kānti and kṣobha show the words being used in verse rather than merely defined, which is the fastest way to hear what register a name belongs to.

references.title: Lalitā-sahasranāma, with Bhāskararāya's commentary Saubhāgyabhāskara
references.author: tr. R. Ananthakrishna Sastry (Theosophical Publishing House, Adyar)
references.note: Useful on this verse for the treatment of kālakaṇṭhī, where a commentator has to decide whether the dark throat is hers by identity with Śiva or by her own act. Watching the reasoning is more instructive than the conclusion, and it shows how much of the hymn's meaning is supplied by the commentator rather than by the text.
